HINDUSTANI VOCAL THEORY

Year 1: Structural Foundations

Semester 1: Fundamental Grammar

Module 1: Basic Vocabulary : Study of Nada, Shruti, Swara (Shuddha/Vikrit), Saptak, and the concept of Laya.

Module 2: Raga Characteristics : Vadi, Samvadi, Anuvadi, Vivadi, Varjya, and Vakra swaras.

Module 3: Thaat & Time Theory : The 10 Thaat system of Pt. Bhatkhande; Classification of Ragas by time (Purvanga/Uttaranga).

Module 4: Raga Lakshana : Detailed study of 5 foundational Ragas (e.g., Yaman, Alhaiya Bilawal, Bhairav).

Methodology: Lecture-demonstrations using the Harmonium/Tanpura for interval identification.

Semester 2: Notation & Classical Forms

Module 1: Notation Systems : Mastery of Pt. V.N. Bhatkhande and Pt. V.D. Paluskar notation for melody and rhythm.

Module 2: Major Vocal Forms : Structural study of Dhrupad, Dhamar, and Khayal (Vilambit/Drut).

Module 3: Secondary Forms : Definition and characteristics of Tarana, Trivat, Chaturang, and Sargam Geet.

Module 4: Early Treatises : Overview of Natyasastra and Dattilam regarding Vocal music.

Methodology: Notation workshops where students transcribe recorded Bandishes.

Year 2: History & Rhythm

Semester 3: Historical Treatises

Module 1: Ancient Era : Study of Matanga’s Brihaddesi and the emergence of the Raga concept.

Module 2: Medieval Era : Sangita Ratnakara of Sharngadeva—an overview of the Saptadhyayi.

Module 3: Transition Period : Swaramela Kalanidhi and the works of Ahobala (Sangit Parijat).

Module 4: Institutionalization : The role of music conferences and the contributions of Pt. Bhatkhande.

Methodology: Comparative textual analysis and student-led seminars on historical shifts.

Semester 4: The Tala System

Module 1: Tala Fundamentals : Matra, Vibhag, Sam, Khali, Tali, and the 10 Pranas of Tala.

Module 2: Major Talas : Study of Teental, Ektal, Jhaptal, Rupak, Chautal, Dhamar.

Module 3: Layakari : Mathematical notation of Dugun, Tigun, Chaugun, and Ari/Kuad ($1.5$ speed).

Module 4: Accompaniment Ethics : Relationship between the vocalist and the Tabla player.

Methodology: Rhythmic drills (clapping/recitation) and mathematical calculation of Tihais.

Year 3: Style & Aesthetics

Module 2: Major Khayal Gharanas : Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Jaipur-Atrauli, Patiala.

Module 3: Stylistic Differences : Analyzing Tan-patterns, Meend, and Kanas across different schools.

Module 4: Biographies : Life and work of Tansen, Sadarang-Adarang, and 20th-century pioneers.

Methodology: Comparative listening using archival audio to identify stylistic markers.

Module 1: Rasa Theory : The Rasa Sutra and its application in Hindustani performance.

Module 2: Semi-Classical Genres : Aesthetics of Thumri, Tappa, Dadra, and Bhajan.

Module 3: Folk Influences : Study of Maand, Baul, and Bhatiyali and their interaction with classical music.

Methodology: Creative workshops on Bhava (expression) and guest artist interactions.

CARNATIC VOCAL THEORY

Program Outcomes (POs)

Upon completion of the 4-year BPA program, students will be able to:

PO1: Demonstrate mastery over the theoretical and practical aspects of Carnatic music.

PO2: Analyze and interpret ancient musical treatises in a modern context.

PO3: Perform complex Manodharma (improvisational) aspects with creative and technical precision.

PO4: Conduct independent research in musicology using standardized methodologies.

PO5: Qualify for competitive academic exams like UGC NET/JRF for higher research.

Theory Syllabus Structure

Total Credits: 3

Total Semester Hours: 45 Hours

Distribution: 4 Modules per Semester

Hours per Module: ~11 Hours

Semester 1: Fundamental Concepts & Melakarta

Course Objectives (COb)

To introduce the technical vocabulary and grammatical foundations of Carnatic music.

To decode the mathematical logic behind the 72 Melakarta system using the Katapayadi formula.

To develop the ability to categorize Ragas based on their structural characteristics.

To understand the evolution of early musical forms from basic exercises to structured compositions.

Course Outcomes (CO)

Upon completion of this course, the student will be able to:

CO1: Define and explain core musical terminologies and the concept of Sangeetha Lakshana.

CO2: Calculate the position and swara nomenclature of any Melakarta raga using the Katapayadi Sankhya.

CO3: Analyze and classify Janya ragas based on their relationship with parent scales.

CO4: Distinguish between various early compositional forms through structural and melodic analysis.

Pedagogy

Classroom Lecture, Audio Demonstrations,

Problem-solving workshops, Logic puzzles

Comparative Analysis, Listening Sessions

Guided listening, Structural mapping

Semester 1: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: Musical Terminology & Sangeetha Lakshana

The Origin of Sound: Study of Nada—classification into Ahata (man-made/struck) and Anahata (natural/unstruck) sounds;   the three levels of sound intensity (Mandhra, Madhya, Tara).

Shruti & Swara: Definition & introduction of the 22 Shrutis (lineage of pitch/microtones) and the 12 Swarasthanas (semitones).

Swara nomenclature: Detailed study of the 12 Swarasthanas and the 16 names (Shodasa Swara); system used in Carnatic music to identify variants of Ri, Ga, Dha, and Ni.

Sthayi & Laya: Understanding Sthayi (octave), and the three speeds of rhythm Laya (tempo; Prathama, Dwitiya, Tritiya), and the concept of Adhara Shadjam.

Course Outcomes – CO1RBT Levels – L1, L2

Module 2: The 72 Melakarta Scheme

Logic of the System: Introduction to the 72 parent ragas as codified by Venkatamakhin.

The Katapayadi Sankhya: The Sanskrit alphanumeric code used to determine a raga's number and notes.

The Chakra System: Classification of the 72 ragas into 12 Chakras (groups of 6), such as Indu, Netra, Agni, etc. Suddha & Prati Madhyama ragas - The division of the scheme into the first 36 (Purva) and the latter 36 (Uttara) Ragas.

Vivadi Swaras: Theoretical understanding of ragas containing dissonant intervals and their placement in the scheme.

Course Outcomes – CO2RBT Levels – L3, L4

Module 3: Raga Classification (Janaka & Janya)

Parent and Derivative Ragas: The characteristics of a "Parent" Raga (Must be Sampurna, have same notes in ascent/descent etc.), relationship between Janaka (parent) and Janya (descendant) ragas.

Janya Raga Sub-types: * Varja Ragas (omitted notes).

Vakra Ragas (Non-linear or zig-zag scales).

Upanga and Bhashanga Ragas that stay strictly within the parent notes versus those that introduce "foreign" notes (Anya Swara).

The Concept of Anya Swara: How specific compositions introduce notes outside the parent scale for aesthetic beauty.

Ghanaraga Panchakam: Introduction and theoretical overview of the five “Ghana” (heavy) ragas (Nata, Gaula, Arabhi, Varali, Sri) traditionally used for deep improvisation.

Course Outcomes – CO3RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 4: Early Compositional Forms

Abhyasa Gana: The educational repertoire of Carnatic music. The sequence of learning—Sarali Varisais, Jantai, Alankaram.

Gitam: Structural analysis of the simplest melodic form; The first melodic composition; study of Pillari and Sanchari Gitams; structural study of Lakshana Gitams (which describe raga grammar) and Lakshya Gitams.

Jatiswaram and Swarajati: Analysis of forms that blend rhythm (Jatis) with melody (Swaras); the transition from technical exercises to performance pieces. Distinguishing between forms that are purely melodic (Jatiswaram) and those that transitioned into dance and storytelling (Swarajati).

Notation Symbols: Introduction to basic Solfa notation: signs for Aksharakala, pauses (Anudrutam), and octave dots.

Course Outcomes – CO4RBT Levels – L2, L5

Methodology for Semester 1:

Mathematical Drills: Using the Katapayadi formula to calculate Raga numbers.

Comparative Listening: Identifying the difference between a Sampurna (complete) and Varja (incomplete) raga.

Notation Training: Writing basic Gitams in the Indian Solfa system.

Learning Resources

Primary Texts: South Indian Music (Volumes I-III) by Prof. P. Sambamoorthy.

Reference Books: The Spiritual Heritage of Tyagaraja by C. Ramanujachari; A Dictionary of South Indian Music by P. Sambamoorthy.

Digital Tools: 'Melakarta' mobile apps for scale visualization; 'Sruti' software for frequency identification.

Multimedia: Recorded archives of the Music Academy, Madras, for authentic demonstrations of early forms.

Suggested Activities

The Katapayadi Challenge: Students are given names of rare Melas and must decode their number and swaras on the spot.

Raga Mapping: Creating a "Family Tree" chart for a specific Melakarta (e.g., Mayamalavagowla) and its popular Janya ragas.

Form Analysis: Listening to a Gitam and a Swarajati and drafting a technical table highlighting the structural differences (Presence of Sahitya, Tala complexity, etc.).

Assessment Details

1. Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) - 30%

Unit Tests (10%): Short descriptive questions on terminology and Mela logic.

Assignments (10%): A research paper on the "Significance of 22 Shrutis in the Melakarta System."

Seminar/Viva (10%): Oral examination on identifying the Chakra and Mela of a given raga name.

2. Semester End Examination (SEE) - 70%

Section A (Recall): Definition of 10 key terms (e.g., Anudhrutam, Vivadi Swara).

Section B (Application): Detailed questions on the construction of the 72 Melakarta chart and the rules of the Katapayadi formula.

Section C (Synthesis/Analysis): Essay-type questions comparing Janaka and Janya ragas or discussing the evolution of the Gitam form.

*********

Semester 2: Notation System, Early History, and Voice Culturing

Course Objectives (Cob)

Cob 1: To master the technicalities of the South Indian musical script and its evolution.

Cob 2: To analyze the life and contributions of Purandara Dasa and early pre-Trinity composers.

Cob 3: To explore the ancient Tamil musical landscape through the literary evidence of Silappadikaram.

Cob 4: To understand the anatomical and physiological basis of voice production and health.

Course Outcomes (CO)

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

CO 1: Transcribe compositions into standardized Carnatic notation with rhythmic and melodic accuracy.

CO 2: Understand the role of the Haridasa movement and early composers in shaping current pedagogical practices.

CO 3: Correlate ancient Tamil Pans and instruments with modern Carnatic equivalents.

CO 4: Apply principles of voice culture to enhance tonal quality and prevent vocal strain.

Pedagogy

Workshop Method: Hands-on transcription sessions from audio to script.

Biographical Inquiry: Researching the sociopolitical context of the Pitamaha.

Interdisciplinary Study: Using literature (Silappadikaram) to extract musicological data.

Demonstration-Performance: Practical sessions on breathing and resonance.

Semester 2: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: The Art and Evolution of South Indian Notation System

Notation Symbols: Mastery of symbols for different octaves (dots above/below), duration (commas, semicolons), and speed divisions. Symbols for first, second, and third speeds (Prathama, Dwitiya, Tritiya Kalam).

Structural Notating: Techniques for notating a Swaravali or a Gitam with correct rhythmic subdivisions. Techniques for writing Varnams and Kritis including Pallavi, Anupallavi, and Charanam demarcations.

Gamaka Representation: Traditional and modern ways of indicating oscillations (Kampita), slides (Jaru), and stress (Spuritham) in text.

Comparative Scripting: A look at how notation has evolved from palm-leaf manuscripts to the standardized modern system. Bhatkhande-style Influence; Adapting symbols for different octaves (Sthayis) and rhythmic pulses (Akshara Kalas).

Course Outcomes – CO1RBT Levels – L3, L6

Module 2: Pitamaha & Early Composers

Purandara Dasa: The “Pitamaha” (Grandfather) of Carnatic music; his role in standardization of the grading system (Sarali to Alankaram); creating the Abhyasa Gana (foundational exercises); his social philosophy and the “Suladi” format.

Tallapaka Annamacharya: The pioneer of the Sankirtana tradition; structural analysis of Pallavi-Charanam format in his Adhyatma and Sringara compositions and his role in the Venkateswara temple tradition.

Dasa Sahitya: The spiritual and social philosophy behind the Devaranamas. How Kanaka Dasa and other used the “Ugabhoga” and “Devaranama” to bridge the gap between classical and folk devotion.

Bhadrachala Ramadasu: His influence on the Kirtana form and the development of devotional music.

Course Outcomes – CO2RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 3: Ancient Tamil Musicology (Silappadikaram)

Exploring the non-Sanskritic roots of South Indian music through Tamil literature.

The Epic of the Anklet: Contextual study of music and dance in Ilango Adigal’s Silappadikaram.

The Pan System: Study of ancient Tamil Pans and their equivalence to modern Ragas (e.g., Sempalaipalai to Harikambhoji).

Vatta-Palai & Yazh: Understanding the ancient circular mapping of notes and the evolution of the Yazh (ancient harp) into the Veena.

Kural, Thutham, Kaikkilai: Nomenclature of the seven notes in the ancient Tamil tradition.

Course Outcomes – CO3RBT Levels – L4, L5

Module 4: Voice Culture & Physiology

Vocal Anatomy: The science of the larynx, the lungs, vocal cords, the role of the diaphragm in breath support, and the sinus cavities in resonance and pitch production.

Sadhakam (Practice) Techniques/Breathing Mechanics: Theoretical study of diaphragmatic breathing and breath-holding (Kumbhaka) for long phrases (Karvai). Traditional methods for developing “Sharira” (voice quality), flexibility, and volume control across three octaves, methods for developing Akara (vowel clarity), Bhruka (humming), and Humkara.

Acoustics of the Voice – Range and Flexibility: Understanding how vowel sounds (Akara, Ikara, Ukara) change the shape of the oral cavity and affect tonal colour. Exercises to increase vocal reach across three octaves (Tristhayi).

Vocal Health: Ayurvedic and modern perspectives on maintaining the voice and preventing strain.

Course Outcomes – CO4RBT Levels – L3

Methodology for Semester 2

Notation Scripting Lab: Converting 17th-century palm-leaf style notation samples into modern standardized script to understand the evolution of symbols.

Comparative Charting: Mapping ancient Tamil Pans to their corresponding modern Melakarta ragas.

Lexical Mapping: Creating a "Tamil-Sanskrit Music Glossary" to correlate terms like Kural with Shadjam or Pan with Raga.

Bio-Acoustic Observation: Using real-time pitch-tracking software to visualize how different vowel shapes (Akara vs. Ikara) affect the harmonic resonance of the voice.

Transcription Workshops: Converting a recorded melodic phrase into a written notation.

Dictation Drills: The teacher sings a phrase, and students must correctly notate it with octave and speed markings.

Biographical Seminars: Student-led discussions on the impact of Purandara Dasa’s standardized teaching system. Comparing the lyrical styles of Purandara Dasa and Annamacharya.

Learning Resources

Primary Text: Sangita Sampradaya Pradarshini (Subbarama Dikshitar) for notation study.

History: The History of South Indian Music by R. Rangaramanuja Ayyangar.

Tamil Musicology: Pancha Marabu and translations of Silappadikaram (Arangetru Kadai).

Science: Voice Culture by S.A.K. Durga.

Suggested Activities

Notation “Translation”: Taking a simple Western melody or a folk song and attempting to write it using Carnatic Solfa notation.

The Dasa Walk: A seminar on how Purandara Dasa structured the Sarali Varisais to build muscle memory in beginners.

The Virtual Museum: Exploring the instruments mentioned in Silappadikaram (like the Yazh) through digital museum archives.

Vocal Mapping: Using a biological chart to identify the diaphragm, vocal folds, and resonators during a practice session.

Assessment Plan

1. Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) - 30%

Notation Lab (10%): A practical test where students must transcribe a recorded 4-line Gitam accurately.

History Presentation (10%): A group presentation on the "Pre-Trinity" era and the evolution of the Kriti form.

Voice Culture Practical (10%): Assessment of breath control and sustained pitch (Akaram) stability.

2. Semester End Examination (SEE) - 70%

Part A (20 Marks): Short questions on notation symbols, Dasa Sahitya, and Tamil Pans.

Part B (30 Marks): Essay on the contribution of Purandara Dasa or the musical significance of the Arangetru Kadai.

Part C (20 Marks): Technical analysis of the human vocal apparatus or the comparative logic between ancient and modern notation.

*********

Semester 3: Tala Dasa Pranas & Rhythmic Geometry

Course Objectives (Cob)

Cob 1: To analyze the ten vital elements (Tala Dasa Pranas) that govern the life and movement of rhythm.

Cob 2: To master the mathematical logic of the 35 Tala Scheme through the permutation of Suladi Sapta Talas and Jati variations.

Cob 3: To understand the concept of Graha (Eduppu) and its role in the aesthetic placement of a composition within a rhythmic cycle.

Cob 4: To explore the visual and structural patterns of Yati and their application in sophisticated melodic and rhythmic designs.

Course Outcomes (CO)

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

CO 1: Evaluate the structural integrity of any Tala based on the Dasa Prana framework.

CO 2: Calculate and demonstrate the total Akshara Kalas of any Tala within the 35-Tala system.

CO 3: Identify and execute different Eduppus (Grahas) in varied compositions to maintain rhythmic equilibrium.

CO 4: Design rhythmic patterns using different Yati structures (Gopucha, Srotovaha, etc.) in both melody and rhythm.

Pedagogy

Mathematical Workshops: Step-by-step derivation of Tala counts using Jati and Gati permutations.

Rhythmic Visualization: Using diagrams to map Yati patterns and Graha placements.

Practical Drills: Hands-on training in keeping “Thalam” while executing complex “Eduppus.”

Comparative Analysis: Studying different compositions to see how “Pranas” like Laya and Marga are applied.

Semester 3: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: The Tala Dasa Pranas

The Ten Life-Breaths: Detailed study of the five physical and five mental aspects of Tala: Kaala, Marga, Kriya, Anga, Graha, Jati, Kalai, Laya, Yati, and Prastara.

Kaala & Marga: Understanding the units of time and the “pathway” of the rhythm (e.g., Dakshina, Vartika, Chitra).

Kriya: Classification into Nishabda (silent) and Sashabda (sounded) movements of the hand.

Angas: Beyond the Shadangas—understanding the role of Anudhrutam, Dhrutam, Laghu, Guru, Plutam, and Kakapadam.

Course Outcomes – CO1 RBT Levels – L2, L5

Module 2: The 35 Tala Scheme & Jati Variations

The Suladi Sapta Talas: Definition and structure of the seven basic talas: Dhruva, Matya, Rupaka, Jhampa, Triputa, Ata, and Eka.

Jati Permutations: The impact of changing the Laghu value (Trisra, Chaturasra, Khanda, Misra, Sankeerna) on the seven talas to create the 35-tala matrix.

The 175 Tala Concept: A theoretical introduction to how the 35 talas expand into 175 through the application of the five Gatis (pulses).

Practical Calculation: Calculating the total Matra and Akshara counts for complex talas like Misra Jati Jhampa Tala or Khanda Jati Ata Tala.

Course Outcomes – CO2 RBT Levels – L3, L4

Module 3: The Concept of Graha (Eduppu) & Its Types

Definition of Graha: The starting point of the song (Sahitya) in relation to the starting point of the Tala cycle.

Sama Graha: When the song and the tala start simultaneously.

Vishama Graha: Detailed study of 

Anagata (song starts after the tala)

Atita (song starts before the tala).

Mathematical Precision: Calculating Eduppu in terms of Matras and Aksharas for various Kritis and Varnams.

Course Outcomes – CO3 RBT Levels – L3, L4

Module 4: Yati and Rhythmic Geometry

The Six Yatis: Structural analysis of rhythmic flow: Sama, Gopucha (cow’s tail), Srotovaha (river flow), Damaru (hourglass), Mridanga (drum shape), and Vishama.

Yati in Sahitya: Examples from Muthuswami Dikshitar’s compositions (e.g., Tyagaraja Yoga Vaibhavam) where words follow geometric patterns.

Yati in Kalpanaswaras: Learning to build rhythmic ending patterns (Korvais) using Srotovaha and Gopucha logic.

Course Outcomes – CO4 RBT Levels – L4, L6

Methodology for Semester 3:

Tala Charting: Creating a visual matrix of the 35 talas with their specific Anga notations.

Eduppu Drills: Listening to 10 different compositions and identifying whether the Graha is Sama or Vishama.

Pattern Design: Students will be asked to write a simple 4-bar rhythmic phrase following a Srotovaha Yati (gradually increasing length).

Mnemonic Recitation (Konnakol): Reciting the Jatis of the 35 talas to internalize the varied Laghu lengths.

Learning Resources

Primary Text: South Indian Music (Book IV) by Prof. P. Sambamoorthy.

Reference: Laya Vadyas by Prof. P. Sambamoorthy.

Digital: ‘Tala Keeper’ apps and metronomes for practice.

Performance Analysis: Videos of Tani Avartanams (percussion solos) to observe Dasa Pranas in action.

Suggested Activities

The Tala Quiz: Identifying the Jati of a Tala based on a provided hand gesture sequence.

Geometric Composition: Writing a short verse where the number of syllables follows a Gopucha Yati (decreasing syllables).

Eduppu Mapping: Using a stopwatch or metronome to mark the exact beat where the Anagata Graha of a popular Kriti falls.

Assessment Plan

Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) – 30%

Mathematical Test (10%): Calculating the Akshara counts for a set of 5 Suladi Talas with mixed Jatis.

Yati Project (10%): Designing a rhythmic Korvai based on the Mridanga Yati pattern.

Practical Viva (10%): Demonstrating the five Jatis through hand gestures while maintaining a constant tempo.

Semester End Examination (SEE) – 70%

Part A (20 Marks): Short technical questions on the names of the Dasa Pranas and Yatis.

Part B (30 Marks): Detailed essay on the 35 Tala Scheme or the classification of Vishama Grahas.

Part C (20 Marks): Solving rhythmic problems involving Matra calculations and Anga notation for specific Talas.

*********

Semester 4: Advanced Compositional Structures, Comparative Study & Manodharma

Course Objectives (Cob)

Cob1: To analyze the architectural complexity of the Varnam as the foundational blueprint for Raga and Tala.

Cob2: To distinguish between the structural and aesthetic nuances of Kirtana and Kriti forms.

Cob3: To perform a comparative analysis of the scales and performance philosophies of Carnatic and Hindustani systems.

Cob4: To establish a theoretical framework for the five branches of Manodharma Sangeetha.

Course Outcomes (CO)

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

CO1: Deconstruct the structural elements of Tana and Pada Varnams and explain their pedagogical significance.

CO2: Identify the evolution of the Kriti form through the contributions of the Trinity and post-Trinity composers.

CO3: Correlate Carnatic Ragas with their Hindustani counterparts and analyze differences in ornamentation.

CO4: Understand the grammatical rules governing Alapana, Kalpanaswara, and Niraval.

Pedagogy

Structure Mapping: Analyzing concert recordings to identify transition points between composed and improvised sections.

Comparative Listening: Side-by-side audio analysis of Carnatic and Hindustani interpretations of similar scales.

Inquiry-Based Learning: Researching the shift from the devotional Kirtana to the art-focused Kriti.

Analytical Transcription: Mapping the mathematical permutations used in professional-level Kalpanaswaras.

Semester 4: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: The Varnam – The Master Architect

Structural Anatomy: Detailed study of Pallavi, Anupallavi, Muktayi Swara, Charanam, and Chittaswaras.

Tana vs. Pada Varnam: Comparing the rhythmic focus and technical speed of Tana Varnams with the melodic, emotive, and Sahitya-rich Pada Varnams used in dance.

Pedagogical Significance: Why the Varnam is considered the “Grammar of the Raga”; its role in developing Gatra Dharma (voice culture) and Tala stability.

Ghanaraga Panchaka Varnams: Introduction to the importance of the five major ragas through the Varnam format.

Course Outcomes – CO1 RBT Levels – L4, L5

Module 2: The Kirtana & Kriti (Devotional & Artistic Forms)

The Kirtana: Evolution of the devotional form; focus on Nama Siddhanta and simple melodic structures; study of Annamayya’s compositions, the Divyanama and Utsava Sampradaya Kirtanas.

The Kriti: The peak of “Art Music”; study of the sophisticated Pallavi-Anupallavi-Charanam structure; the introduction of Sangatis (variations) by Tyagaraja.

Post-Trinity Innovations: Study of the Swara-sahitya, Madhyamakala Sahitya, and Chittaswaras added to Kritis to enhance complexity.

Lyrical Components: Understanding the role of Mudra (composer’s signature), Prosody (Prasa, Yati, Anuprasa), and Rasa.

Course Outcomes – CO2 RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 3: Comparative Study: Carnatic vs. Hindustani

Systemic Overlap: Historical divergence of the two systems; identifying common roots in ancient texts (13th-14th Century).

Scale Systems: 

Comparing the 72 Melakarta (mathematical) system of the South with the 10 Thaat (classification-based) system of the North. 

Comparative study of major scales: Sankarabharanam vs. Bilawal, Mayamalavagowla vs. Bhairav, Kalyani vs. Yaman, Todi vs. Bhairavi.

Rhythmic Structures: 

Detailed study of Tala vs. Taal; 

The concept of the Laghu (variable) vs. the Theka (fixed patterns).

Performance Aesthetics: 

Comparison of the Katcheri format vs. the Khayal format; 

The difference between Gamaka (oscillations) and Meend (glides).

Terminology Translation: Mapping Southern terms to Northern equivalents (e.g., Mela to Thaat, Tala to Taal, Sruti to Sur).

Course Outcomes – CO3 RBT Levels – L4, L5

Module 4: The Grammar of Manodharma & Introduction to Advanced Improvisation

The Five Branches: 

Theoretical introduction to Raga Alapana, Niraval, Kalpanaswara, Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi (RTP), and Pallavi.

Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi (RTP) Overview: Brief theoretical introduction to the pinnacle of Manodharma.

Alapana Paddhati: The stages of Raga exploration—Akshiptika (Introduction), Ragavardhani (Expansion), Makharini (Conclusion), Vidari, and Sthayi.

Kalpanaswaras (Swarakalpana):

Sarvalaghu: Flowing, natural rhythmic patterns.

Kanakkus: Mathematical, calculated rhythmic patterns ending in Tihais or Korvais. 

Introduction to Sarvalaghu (flow-based) vs. Kanaka-Rakta (calculated) swara permutations.

Ethics of Improvisation: 

Maintaining the Raga Swaroopa while exploring creativity; the role of the accompanist during Manodharma.

Understanding the “Dos and Don’ts” of staying within a Raga’s identity during spontaneous singing.

Course Outcomes – CO4 RBT Levels – L2, L3

Methodology for Semester 4:

Concert Deconstruction: Students will listen to a 90-minute concert and timestamp every transition from Kalpita (composed) to Manodharma (improvised) music.

Raga Comparison Project: Developing a chart that lists 10 Carnatic Ragas alongside their Hindustani equivalents and noting three distinct differences in phrasing.

Structural Charting: Creating a visual map of a heavy Tyagaraja Kriti showing the progression of Sangatis.

Improvisation Journal: Writing down five potential Niraval lines from known Kritis and justifying why they are rhythmically suitable.

Learning Resources

Primary Text: South Indian Music (Book V) by Prof. P. Sambamoorthy.

Reference: The Ragas of North India by Walter Kaufmann; Great Composers by P. Sambamoorthy.

Digital: Comparative playlists on Spotify/YouTube featuring artists like M.S. Subbulakshmi and Pt. Bhimsen Joshi on similar ragas.

Suggested Activities

The “Mela-Thaat” Quiz: Fast-paced identification of the Hindustani Thaat for a given Carnatic Melakarta.

Varnam Analysis: Taking a notation of a Varnam and circling the Jiva Swaras (life-giving notes) highlighted in the Muktayi Swara section.

Sangati Tracking: Singing a simple line and creating four different Sangatis that progressively increase in melodic complexity.

Assessment Plan

1. Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) - 30%

Comparative Essay (10%): A 1000-word paper on "The influence of the Persian system on the Hindustani-Carnatic divide."

Structural Analysis Test (10%): Identifying the parts of a Varnam or Kriti from a provided notation sheet.

Viva Voce (10%): Explaining the rules of Raga Alapana for a specific chosen Raga.

2. Semester End Examination (SEE) - 70%

Part A (20 Marks): Short questions on the definitions of Mudra, Sangati, Thaat, and Manodharma.

Part B (30 Marks): Essay questions comparing Kirtana and Kriti or Tana and Pada Varnams.

Part C (20 Marks): Technical mapping of the Dasa Vidha Gamakas in a specific Varnam or comparing the treatment of Raga Kalyani across both Indian systems.

Semester 5: The Historical Treatises, Raga Lakshanas & The Trinity

Course Objectives (COb)

COb1: To master the standardized technical profile (Raga Lakshana) of major, minor, and rare Ragas.

COb2: To analyze the historical evolution of musicology through a chronological study of Treatises and Lexicons.

COb3: To evaluate the life, distinct musical styles, and transformative contributions of the Musical Trinity and their disciples.

COb4: To decode the hidden identities and poetic significance of Vaggeyakara Mudras and composer signatures.

Course Outcomes (CO)

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

CO1: Document and present a detailed technical profile of any given Raga, including its Arohana-Avarohana, Jiva Swaras, and Sancharas.

CO2: Compare and contrast the theories presented in seminal texts like the Natya Shastra, Brihaddesi, and Swaramelakalanidhi.

CO3: Distinguish between the compositional "banis" (styles) of Tyagaraja, Muthuswami Dikshitar, and Syama Sastri.

CO4: Identify the composer of a Kriti by analyzing its Ankita Mudra and structural characteristics.

Pedagogy

Lexicon Research: Mapping modern Raga identities to ancient definitions found in historical treatises.

Biographical Deconstruction: Study of the Trinity's life through the lens of their specific compositional "blueprints" (e.g., Ghana Ragas vs. Vibhakti Kritis).

Lakshana Workshops: Collaborative building of Raga "Bio-data" files using historical and contemporary sources.

Signature Hunting: Analyzing lyrical texts to find subtle or hidden Mudras across different centuries of composers.

Semester 5: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: Historical Treatises & Lexicons

Ancient Era: Study of Bharata’s Natya Shastra (concept of Jaati and Gramas) and Matanga’s Brihaddesi (the first definition of "Raga").

Medieval Era: Analysis of Sarngadeva’s Sangita Ratnakara and Ramamatya’s Swaramelakalanidhi (evolution of the Mela concept).

Modern Bridge: Somanatha’s Ragavibodha and Govinda’s Sangraha Chudamani (the 72 Melakarta scheme refinement).

Lexical Evolution: How the terminology of the Shruti and Swara shifted through these texts over a millennium.

Course Outcomes – CO2 RBT Levels – L4, L5

Module 2: Raga Lakshana (Standard Raga Study)

Technical Parameters: Detailed study of Arohana-Avarohana, Varjya/Vakra patterns, and classification (Upanga/Bhashanga).

The main Characteristics of a Raga: 

Raga Dasa Lakshanas as per Bharata’s Natya Sastra (4th Century B.C.) and 

Raga Trayodasa Lakshanas as per the Sarangadeva’s Sangita Ratnakara (13th Century A.D.). 

Understanding Graha, amsa, tara, mandra, nyasa, apanyasa, sanyasa, vinyasa, bahutva, alpatva, antara marga, shadava and audava.

Standard Study of Ragas: Extensive profile building for:

Major Ragas: Todi, Sankarabharanam, Kalyani, Bhairavi, Kambhoji.

Janya & Minor Ragas: Mohanam, Hamsadhwani, Anandabhairavi, Sahana, Ritigowla.

Sanchara Documentation: Writing characteristic phrases that define the Swaroopa (personality) of the Raga.

Course Outcomes – CO1 RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 3: The Trinity of Carnatic Music and the Post-Trinity Era

Tyagaraja: Mastery of the Kriti format and melodic variations (Sangatis); the use of Sangatis and the emphasis on Bhakti and Rama Nama. (The Naukacharitram and Prahlada Bhakti Vijayam.)

Muthuswami Dikshitar: The Vibhakti Kritis and Navagraha series; the Vainika style of vocalization and extensive use of Madhyamakala Sahitya. Raga-Mudras and the Gopucha/Srotovaha Yati applications.

Syama Sastri: The architect of rhythm; mastery of Misra Chapu Tala and the Swarajati form (Ratnatrayam).

The Post-Trinity Influence: Study of the disciples (The Sishya Parampara) and composers like Swati Tirunal, Patnam Subramania Iyer, and Papanasam Sivan.

Course Outcomes – CO3 RBT Levels – L2, L4 

Module 4: Vaggeyakara Mudras & Signatures

Types of Mudras: Understanding the different "stamps":

Ankita Mudra: Composer's name/pen-name (e.g., Guruguha, Tyagaraja, Syama Krishna).

Raga Mudra: Mention of the Raga name within the lyrics.

Tala Mudra: Mention of the Tala within the composition.

Vageyakara Mudra: Identifying the specific poetic style unique to a composer.

Vamsa/Guru Mudra: References to their lineage or spiritual teacher (e.g., Guruguha for Dikshitar).

Kshetra Mudra: Naming the specific temple or location for which the song was composed (e.g., Kanchi, Srirangam).

Prabandha Mudra: Indicators of the song's structural type or rhythm.

Historical Survey: Signatures of pre-Trinity (Annamacharya, Purandara Dasa) versus modern composers (Balamuralikrishna, Lalgudi Jayaraman).

Significance: The role of Mudras in authenticating compositions and preserving authorship in an oral tradition.

Course Outcomes – CO4 RBT Levels – L2, L3

Methodology for Semester 5:

Treatise Timeline: Creating a visual infographic or timeline showing the evolution of musical theory from Jaati to Raga.

The "Style Guide" Project: Comparing three compositions in the same Raga (e.g., Bhairavi) by each of the Trinity to identify their unique stylistic markers.

Lakshana Lab: Students present a "Raga Profile" using both theoretical notation and practical demonstration of key Sancharas.

Mudra Decoding: A competitive exercise identifying the composer of unknown lyrics based solely on the Ankita Mudra. 

Library Research: Identifying 10 Raga Mudras and 10 Ankita Mudras from the Kriti collections in the music library.

Learning Resources

Primary Text: South Indian Music (Book IV & V) by Prof. P. Sambamoorthy.

Reference: The Chaturdandi Prakashika of Venkatamakhin; Composers of the Trinity by various authors (Music Academy publications).

Digital: 'Kriti Archive' websites and audio databases for comparative Banis.

Suggested Activities

The Trinity Trivia: Identifying a composition by hearing only the Chittaswara or a specific Madhyamakala phrase.

Lexicon Cross-Reference: Looking up a Raga in the Sangita Sampradaya Pradarshini and comparing its notes with the modern version.

Mudra Hunt: Scanning a sheet of 20 Kritis to highlight and categorize every Mudra found (Raga, Tala, or Composer).

Assessment Plan

1. Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) - 30%

Treatise Review (10%): A written comparison of any two major historical texts.

Raga Lakshana Folder (10%): Submission of five comprehensive Raga Bio-data sheets.

Listening Viva (10%): Identifying the composer of a recording based on stylistic markers and Mudras.

2. Semester End Examination (SEE) - 70%

Part A (20 Marks): Short technical questions on Dasa Lakshanas and specific composer Mudras.

Part B (30 Marks): Essay questions on the contribution of a specific member of the Trinity or the evolution of the Mela theory across treaties.

Part C (20 Marks): Detailed Raga Lakshana description of a major Mela and its Janya derivatives.

Semester 6: The Modern Concert (Katcheri)

Course Objectives (COb)

COb1: To trace the historical transition of Carnatic music from royal court patronage to the modern democratic Sabha system.

COb2: To understand the technical and ethical dynamics of the ensemble, specifically the supportive roles of the Violin and Mridangam.

COb3: To explore the psychological and aesthetic application of Rasa (emotion) and Bhava (expression) in a live performance context.

COb4: To master the strategic principles of Katcheri Dharma (concert ethics and planning) for professional stage presentation.

Course Outcomes (CO)

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

CO1: Analyze the impact of modernization and acoustics on concert formats and vocal techniques.

CO2: Evaluate the collaborative relationship between the lead performer and accompanists during various stages of a concert.

CO3: Apply aesthetic principles to evoke specific emotional responses through Raga and Sahitya selection.

CO4: Design a professionally balanced concert repertoire (Katcheri Paddyathi) suited for different durations and audiences.

Pedagogy

Historical Mapping: Reviewing archival records and oral histories to track the shift in performance spaces.

Ensemble Simulation: Mock concert sessions where students rotate roles to understand the perspective of accompanists.

Aesthetic Analysis: Deep-listening sessions focused on identifying the Rasas intended by composers and interpreted by performers.

Repertoire Curation Workshops: Practical exercises in building concert lists based on temporal and thematic constraints.

Semester 6: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: The Modern Concert Era - Evolution & Innovation

The Transition of Patronage: The shift from the Tanjore and Mysore royal courts to the mercantile and intellectual "Sabhas" of Madras (Chennai).

Democratization of Art: How the transition to public Sabhas influenced Raga selection, time management, and the shortening of elaborate Ragam-Tanam-Pallavis.

The Music Academy & Institutionalization: The role of the 1927 Madras Music Conference in codifying theory and establishing the "December Season" as a global cultural event.

Musical Acoustics & Innovation: 

The physics of the acoustics of modern venues and the evolution of the Sangeetha Sabha culture. 

The modern concert hall; sound absorption, reflection, and the impact of electronic amplification on vocal "close-mic" techniques.

Evolution from the manual Tambura to electronic Sruti boxes and apps; the impact of recording formats (78 RPM records & LP discs to digital) on composition length.

Modern digital archiving and the role of social media/streaming in the global spread of Carnatic music.

Course Outcomes – CO1 RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 2: The Art of Accompaniment & Concert Ethics

The melodic accompaniment’s Role: 

Techniques of "following/shadowing" the vocalist; 

The ethics of the solo turn in Alapana and Swara; maintaining melodic fidelity. 

Ethics of mimicking vs. complementing the main artist.

The percussion accompaniment’s Role: 

The role of the Mridangam, Ghatam, and Khanjira;

Providing rhythmic "Sarvalaghu" support; 

The art of the Gumki; anticipation of Eduppus and the structure of the Tani Avartanam (percussion solo).

Ensemble Hierarchy: Understanding the unspoken cues between the lead artist and the "Upapakkavadyams" (Ghatam, Kanjira, Morsing).

Platform Etiquette: Stage presence, seating arrangements,microphone etiquette, and the mutual respect required for a successful collaborative performance.

Supporting the Manodharma: How a melodic accompanists and percussionist respond to spontaneous Alapana and Kalpanaswaras.

Course Outcomes – CO2 RBT Levels – L3, L5

Module 3: Concepts of Rasa and Bhava in Performance

Rasa Theory: Study of the Nava Rasas (Nine Emotions) and their specific manifestation in Carnatic Ragas (e.g., Karuna in Sahana, Veera in Atana).

Bhava (Expression): 

The difference between Vachika (lyrical) and Angika (physical/expressive) Bhava; 

Distinguishing between Vibhava (cause), Anubhava (physical effect), and Sanchari Bhava (fleeting emotions) within a song.

The role of Aparoksha Anubhava (direct experience) of the composer.

Raga-Rasa Correspondence: 

Scientific and psychological theories on why certain intervals evoke specific moods.

The role of lyrics in evoking emotion; the concept of Dhwani (suggestive meaning) in the compositions of the Trinity.

The Performer-Audience Bridge: 

The concept of Sahridaya (the empathetic listener) and the transfer of emotion from the stage to the gallery.

Techniques for using Gamakas and Kaku (voice modulation) to enhance the emotional delivery of a Kriti.

Course Outcomes – CO3 RBT Levels – L3, L4

Module 4: Principles of Concert Planning (Katcheri Dharma)

The Ariyakudi Revolution: In-depth study of Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar and the standardization of the Katcheri Paddhati (the modern concert sequence).

The Anatomy of a Concert List:

The Opening: Selecting a Varnam or a brisk Ganapathi Kriti to establish the Sruti and tempo.

The Middle (Main/Sub-main): Balancing heavy Ragas (Todi, Kalyani) with medium-paced pieces.

The Pinnacle: Theoretical placement of the Ragam-Tanam-Pallavi (RTP).

The Conclusion: Thukkadas (lighter pieces), Padams, Jawalis, Tillanas, and the Mangalam.

Repertoire Selection: 

Balancing "Heavy" (Ghanam) Ragas with "Pratimadhyama" Ragas; 

Principles of selecting compositions in different Talas (beats), Eduppus (starting points), and Gatis (rhythmic pulses) to avoid monotony and different composers to ensure variety.

Time Management: 

Adapting a concert list for a 60-minute, 90-minute, or 3-hour slot; 

The "Golden Ratio" of Manodharma vs. Kalpita music.

Katcheri Dharma (Ethics): 

Mutual respect between the vocalist and the instrumentalists.

The art of providing space for the Tani Avartanam (percussion solo).

Understanding the audience profile and the occasion (Temple, Wedding, or Sabha).

Course Outcomes – CO4 RBT Levels – L4, L6

Methodology for Semester 6:

Acoustics Lab: Experimenting with singing in different spaces (reverberant vs. dampened) to understand the role of the ear-monitor and room acoustics.

The "Shadowing" Project: Attending a live concert and specifically mapping the interaction (eye contact, cues) between the vocalist and the violinist.

Rasa Profiling: Creating a chart for 10 common Ragas and documenting the dominant Rasa and the specific Prayogas (phrases) that trigger it.

Mock Katcheri: Curating and defending a 45-minute concert list before a panel of peers.

Learning Resources

Primary Text: South Indian Music (Book VI) by Prof. P. Sambamoorthy.

Reference: Between Two Tanpuras by Vamanrao Deshpande (for aesthetic comparison); The Art of Accompaniment (various journal articles).

Digital: Multi-track concert recordings that allow students to isolate the Violin or Mridangam tracks.

Suggested Activities

The "Ariyakudi" Challenge: Reconstructing a concert list based on the archives of the 1940s and comparing it to a modern 2020s concert list.

Microphone Workshop: Practicing distance control and volume modulation with a professional PA system.

Emotion Match: Playing a Raga Alapana and having classmates guess the intended Rasa based on the performer's treatment.

Assessment Plan

1. Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) - 30%

Accompaniment Critique (10%): A written report analyzing the supportive role of the violinist in a selected professional recording.

Repertoire Draft (10%): Designing a themed concert list (e.g., "The compositions of Syama Sastri") with a full justification of the sequence.

Viva Voce (10%): Discussing the application of Katcheri Dharma in high-pressure performance scenarios.

2. Semester End Examination (SEE) - 70%

Part A (20 Marks): Short questions on Rasa names, Katcheri sequence, and the role of the Gumki.

Part B (30 Marks): Essay questions on the evolution of the Sabha system or the psychological link between Raga and Emotion.

Part C (20 Marks): Designing a full 2.5-hour concert list including Tala, Raga, Composer, and Manodharma details.

Semester 7: Musicology, Teaching & Research Aptitude

Course Objectives (COb)

COb1: To introduce the formal principles and methodologies of academic research specifically tailored for musicological studies.

COb2: To develop essential teaching and research competencies required for the UGC NET Paper 1 framework.

COb3: To master logical reasoning and understand the structural evolution of the Indian Higher Education system.

COb4: To apply research tools in documenting, analyzing, and preserving musical traditions through fieldwork and archival study.

Course Outcomes (CO)

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

CO1: Formulate a research problem and design a structured thesis proposal in musicology.

CO2: Apply pedagogical theories and research ethics in an academic environment.

CO3: Analyze logical arguments and navigate the regulatory landscape of Indian higher education.

CO4: Conduct primary and secondary research using field documentation techniques and bibliographic analysis.

Pedagogy

Seminar-Based Learning: Student-led discussions on contemporary research papers in Indian musicology.

Mock UGC NET Drills: Regular practice sessions focusing on Paper 1 reasoning and general awareness.

Case Study Method: Analyzing successful musicological dissertations to understand structural flow.

Problem-Solving Workshops: Using Venn diagrams and syllogisms to strengthen logical reasoning skills.

Semester 7: Module-wise Detailed Syllabus

Module 1: Research Methodology in Music

Fundamentals of Musicology: 

Defining the field; 

Distinguishing between historical musicology, ethnomusicology, and systematic musicology.

Types of research (Historical, Analytical, Experimental); 

Tools of research; 

Research Design: 

Identification of research gaps; 

Formulating a hypothesis; 

Selecting appropriate qualitative and quantitative methods for music research.

Data Sources: Primary sources (Manuscripts, inscriptions, oral traditions) vs. Secondary sources (Books, journals, digital archives).

Thesis Formatting: The structural components of a dissertation—Introduction, Literature Review, Methodology, Analysis, and Conclusion.

Course Outcomes – CO1 RBT Levels – L3, L6

Module 2: Teaching & Research Aptitude (Paper 1 Core)

Teaching Aptitude: 

Concepts, objectives, and levels of teaching; 

Characteristics of learners; 

Factors affecting teaching; offline vs. online teaching methods (SWAYAM, MOOCs).

Research Aptitude: 

Meaning and types of research; 

Steps of research; 

Thesis and article writing.

Research Ethics: Understanding plagiarism, intellectual property rights (IPR), and the ethical considerations of interviewing living artists.

ICT in Research: 

Using software tools for data analysis, citation management (Mendeley/Zotero), and digital music archiving.

Application of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in research; 

Course Outcomes – CO2 RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 3: Logical Reasoning & Higher Education System (Paper 1 Core)

Logical Reasoning: 

Understanding the structure of arguments; 

Deductive and inductive reasoning; 

Venn diagrams; 

Indian Logic (Pramanas)—Pratyaksha, Anumana, Upamana, Shabda.

Higher Education Evolution: Ancient Indian education (Gurukula, Takshashila, Nalanda) and the transition to modern university systems.

Regulatory Framework: The role of the UGC, AIU, NAAC, and the National Education Policy (NEP) in shaping arts and music education.

Professional Education: Technical, vocational, and value-based education within the creative arts sector.

Course Outcomes – CO3 RBT Levels – L2, L4

Module 4: Musicological Research & Fieldwork Techniques

Fieldwork Documentation: Techniques for high-fidelity audio/video recording; conducting structured and semi-structured interviews with veteran musicians.

Primary Source Analysis: Deciphering notation in palm-leaf manuscripts or 19th-century print; authenticating rare compositions.

Bibliographic Studies: Compiling an annotated bibliography; understanding citation styles (APA, MLA, Chicago) relevant to musicology.

Organology & Iconography Research: Methodology for studying instrument evolution through temple sculptures and paintings.

Course Outcomes – CO4 RBT Levels – L4, L5

Methodology for Semester 7:

Proposal Drafting: Students must select a potential research topic and submit a 5-page formal research proposal.

NET Paper 1 Simulations: Weekly timed tests covering Logical Reasoning and Teaching Aptitude.

Field Interview Simulation: A practical exercise where students interview a peer as an "artist" and document the session according to research standards.

Plagiarism Workshop: Learning to use software like Urkund/Turnitin and practicing paraphrasing and citation.

Learning Resources

Primary Text: Research Methodology in Music by Dr. S.A.K. Durga; UGC NET/JRF: Teaching and Research Aptitude by K.V.S. Madaan.

Reference: The Study of Ethnomusicology by Bruno Nettl; Higher Education in India (UGC Publications).

Digital: Access to JSTOR, Shodhganga, and the Oxford Music Online database.

Suggested Activities

The "Pramana" Debate: A classroom debate where students must use Indian logical structures to argue a point in music theory.

Literature Review Hunt: Finding five different scholarly articles on a single Raga and summarizing the conflicting theories found within them.

Digital Archiving: A workshop on cataloguing old cassettes or LP records into a digital database with metadata.

Assessment Plan

1. Continuous Internal Evaluation (CIE) - 30%

Research Proposal (15%): A formal document outlining a potential Year 4 dissertation topic.

Reasoning Quiz (10%): A test focused on logical reasoning and Higher Education structures.

Ethics Seminar (5%): A presentation on the importance of copyright and credit in oral traditions.

2. Semester End Examination (SEE) - 70%

Part A (20 Marks): Objective questions following the UGC NET Paper 1 pattern.

Part B (30 Marks): Essay-type questions on research design or the evolution of Indian higher education.

Part C (20 Marks): Technical questions on research ethics, citation styles, and primary source analysis in musicology.

Execution & Analysis: 

Refining the research question and finalizing the chapter outline.

Applying analytical tools (melodic/rhythmic/textual) to the research subject.

Mechanical, performance, and synchronization rights.

Methods for teaching group classes versus one-on-one Gurukula style.

Evaluation Metrics: 

Creating objective and subjective assessment tools for music theory and practice.

Creating grading rubrics for practical music exams and conducting Viva Voce.

Psychology of Music Learning: Identifying and addressing common student plateaus and performance anxiety.

Module 4: UGC NET & JRF Intensive Review

Paper 1 (General): Final drills on Teaching Aptitude, Research Ethics, and Higher Education Systems.

Paper 2 (Music): 

Units I-III: Historical evolution, ancient treatises, and terminologies.

Teaching Practicum: Students are required to document 10 hours of supervised teaching at the undergraduate level.

Legal Workshop: Drafting a sample "No Objection Certificate" (NOC) and a "Performance Contract" for a hypothetical concert.

Daily NET Drills: Solving 20 MCQs daily with a focus on negative marking avoidance and logic-based elimination.

Portfolio Building: Creating a professional website or digital profile showcasing their performance and academic work.
